analogy.p: Imagine a car driving diagonally from a smooth road into a muddy field. The wheel on the field side hits the mud first and slows down while the other wheel is still on the road at full speed, so the car swings round and its direction changes towards the line perpendicular to the edge of the field (the normal). This is exactly what a wavefront of light does as it enters glass: the part of the wavefront that enters first slows down, so the wavefront turns and the ray bends towards the normal. When the car leaves the mud, the first wheel speeds up and the car swings back, so it ends up travelling in its original direction (but shifted sideways), like the emergent ray in the glass block. The analogy breaks down because a car is a solid object with two wheels, whereas light is a continuous wave with a whole wavefront and a car does not keep the same frequency of wheel rotation.
analogy.t: A car driving from a road onto a muddy field

bullets: The two linked investigations are: (1) **reflection** of a ray of light at a plane mirror and at other surfaces; (2) **refraction** of a ray of light as it passes through a transparent block (glass, Perspex or a water-filled block).
Aim for reflection: to test the **law of reflection**, that the **angle of incidence = angle of reflection**, both measured from the **normal**.
Aim for refraction: to find how the **angle of refraction r** depends on the **angle of incidence i** when light goes from **air into a denser transparent material** and back out again.

You may be asked to describe the **method**, name the **independent, dependent and control variables**, identify **risks**, suggest **improvements**, or **plot and interpret a graph** of your results.
This practical is worth marks in **Paper 2** (waves topic) and the working scientifically skills (method, accuracy, precision, evaluation) can be tested on any practical.

Command words to expect: **describe** (give the steps in order), **explain** (give reasons using ideas about waves), **suggest** (apply knowledge to a new situation), **evaluate** (weigh strengths and weaknesses).
Link to other topics: the same ideas explain **mirrors, lenses, optical fibres, periscopes and prisms**, so a strong understanding here supports many exam questions.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know and do
core.p: This is **AQA required practical 8 (physics)**. The specification statement is to **investigate the reflection of light by different types of surface and the refraction of light by different substances**. You are expected to be able to carry out the method safely, record angles accurately, draw ray diagrams and graphs from your own results, and then answer questions about the method, the variables, the accuracy and the conclusions. The theory behind it (laws of reflection, refraction as a change of wave speed) is examined too, and exam questions often describe a slightly different set-up from the one you did in class, so you must understand why each step is done rather than memorise a script.

bullets: **Ray box** with a single slit and a 12 V (low voltage) supply: produces a thin ray of light; the narrower the slit, the more precise the line you can mark.
**Plane mirror** (with a stand or block of Blu-Tack/modelling clay), plus other surfaces to compare such as **white paper, matt black card, shiny metal foil**.
**Rectangular glass block** (and optionally a **Perspex block** or a **water-filled block**) for refraction.
**Sheet of plain A3/A4 paper** to work on so the ray path can be drawn and kept as a record.
**Sharp pencil** and **ruler** to mark crosses and join them up with straight lines.
**Protractor** (reading to 1° or 0.5°) to measure the angles from the normal; check the zero line is on the normal.
**Power pack**, leads and a **darkened room** or shaded area so that the ray is easy to see against the paper.
Optional: a **set square** to draw the normal exactly at 90° to the boundary, and a **second pair of eyes** to make marking the ray easier.
core.h: Equipment and what each item is for
core.p: A good method names every piece of equipment and its purpose. The key apparatus is a **ray box** (a light source with a single slit or a slit-and-slot plate) which produces a **thin, bright, narrow beam** that you can see on paper. A narrow beam matters because you need to mark the path of the ray precisely; a wide beam would give a wide band, so the angle could not be measured accurately. The other items let you draw lines, mark positions, and measure angles with small uncertainty.

bullets: 1. Draw a straight line across the middle of the paper; place the **mirror** along this line so the reflecting surface is exactly on the line. Mark the position of the mirror.
2. Use a protractor or set square to draw a **normal** at 90° to the mirror at the centre of the line (the **point of incidence**).
3. Draw several **incident rays** onto the point of incidence at chosen angles to the normal, e.g. 10°, 20°, 30°, 40°, 50°, 60°, 70°.
4. Point the ray box so that the ray travels **along one of the drawn lines** onto the mirror; the light should hit the point of incidence.
5. Mark the **reflected ray** with two or more small crosses well spaced along it.
6. Remove the mirror and the ray box; use a ruler to join the crosses to the point of incidence to draw the **reflected ray**.
7. Measure the **angle of incidence i** (between incident ray and normal) and the **angle of reflection r** (between reflected ray and normal) with the protractor.
8. Repeat for each angle and record the results in a table (columns: i/°, r/°).
core.h: Method A: investigating reflection at a plane mirror
core.p: The idea is to send a ray at the mirror at a known angle of incidence and then record where the reflected ray goes. The key skill is measuring both angles **from the normal**, not from the surface of the mirror. Marking the ray with crosses and joining them afterwards with a ruler avoids having to measure a thick, blurry beam directly, which improves accuracy. Repeating at several angles allows you to see a pattern and to spot any anomalous result.

bullets: 1. Place the **glass block** on a sheet of paper and **draw around it** carefully with a sharp pencil.
2. Remove the block, draw a **normal** at 90° to one long side at a point near the middle of that side (the point of entry).
3. Use a protractor to draw an **incident ray** at an angle i of e.g. 20° to the normal, ending at the point of entry.
4. Replace the block exactly in its outline; shine the ray from the ray box along the incident line.
5. Mark the position where the ray **leaves** the opposite side of the block with a cross; also mark a second cross further along the emergent ray.
6. Remove the block; join the two emergent crosses to draw the **emergent ray** and extend it back to the block outline to find the **exit point**.
7. Join the **point of entry** to the **exit point** with a straight line: this is the **refracted ray** inside the block.
8. Measure the **angle of refraction r** (between the refracted ray and the normal at the entry point). Repeat for i = 20°, 30°, 40°, 50°, 60°, 70° and record i and r.
core.h: Method B: investigating refraction through a rectangular block
core.p: Here the ray enters a transparent block, bends at the boundary because its **speed changes**, travels in a straight line through the block, and bends again as it leaves. You cannot see the ray inside the block clearly, so the trick is to mark where the ray **enters** and where it **leaves**, then join those two points after removing the block to find the path **inside** the block. The refracted ray inside the block is the one you measure the angle of refraction r on.

bullets: Typical results: i = 10°, 20°, 30°, 40°, 50°, 60°, 70° give r within ±1 or 2° of the same value.

On a graph of **r against i** the line of best fit passes through (0, 0) and has gradient **1**; if a point is far off the line it is an **anomalous result** (probably a measurement or marking error) and should be repeated.
If the angle is measured from the surface instead of the normal, you would get the **wrong value (90° − i)**; this is the most common error in this practical.

A **very rough surface** (e.g. white paper) gives **diffuse reflection**: the ray scatters in many directions and is not a single narrow beam, so you cannot measure r precisely; only a **smooth shiny surface** (mirror) gives clear **specular reflection** and a clear reflected ray.
A **matt black** surface reflects very little light and absorbs most of it, so the reflected ray is faint; this shows that surfaces differ in how much they reflect and absorb.
Because the angle between the incident ray and reflected ray is **2 × i**, a quick check on your data is that the total angle between the two rays is twice the angle of incidence.

Link to the theory: the law holds for **all waves** (sound, water, light), and the same equation explains echoes and why a plane mirror image appears the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front.
core.h: Results for reflection: what you should find and why
core.p: For every smooth, flat reflecting surface you will find that the **angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence**, within the uncertainty of the protractor. This is the **law of reflection**. If you plot a graph of r against i the points lie close to a **straight line through the origin with a gradient of 1**. The reason is that a wavefront reflecting from a smooth surface keeps the same speed and the same wavelength, so the geometry makes the two angles equal. Small differences (for example 38° and 40°) are due to **measurement uncertainty**, not to the law failing.

bullets: Typical results for glass: i = 20°, 30°, 40°, 50°, 60° give r ≈ 13°, 19°, 25°, 31°, 35°; r is always smaller than i.

The graph of r against i is a **curve** (not a straight line through the origin), because r is **not directly proportional** to i; extension: **sin i divided by sin r is constant** for a given material (the refractive index), but this is beyond GCSE.
Entering glass: ray bends **towards** the normal. Leaving glass: ray bends **away from** the normal.
The emergent ray is **parallel** to the incident ray because the two boundaries are parallel and the bending at the second boundary exactly reverses the bending at the first.
At **normal incidence** (i = 0°) the ray goes straight through with **no change in direction**, although the speed still changes.
The **frequency stays the same** when a wave is refracted; the speed and wavelength change by the same factor (v = f × λ).
Different materials bend light by different amounts: **water bends light less than glass**; the denser (slower) the material for light, the more the ray bends.
Link to the theory: refraction is the reason a straw looks bent in water, a pool looks shallower than it is, and lenses can focus light.
core.h: Results for refraction: what you should find and why
core.p: When light travels from **air into glass** (a more optically dense material) it **slows down** and bends **towards the normal**, so the angle of refraction r is **smaller** than the angle of incidence i. When the ray leaves the block, it travels from glass into air, **speeds up** and bends **away from the normal**, so the emergent ray is **parallel to the incident ray** but **shifted sideways** (a lateral displacement). If the ray travels **along the normal** (i = 0°) it is not deviated at all, because the whole wavefront slows down at the same time. Refraction happens because the wave's **speed changes**, which changes the wavelength while the frequency stays the same.

bullets: **Independent variable (reflection):** the **angle of incidence i**, or (in a comparison of surfaces) the **type of surface**.
**Dependent variable (reflection):** the **angle of reflection r** (or the brightness of the reflected ray when comparing surfaces).
**Independent variable (refraction):** the **angle of incidence i** (or the material of the block).
**Dependent variable (refraction):** the **angle of refraction r** (or the amount the ray is deviated).

**Control variables:** the same **ray box and slit** (same beam width), same **block or mirror**, same **point of incidence**, same **protractor** and same measuring method, same **wavelength (colour) of light**, same **room lighting**.
Keeping the **colour (wavelength) of light** the same matters because different wavelengths are refracted by slightly different amounts (this is why a prism splits white light).
A **fair test** changes one variable at a time; if you change both the block and the angle you cannot tell which caused the change in r.
**Resolution** of the protractor is 1° (or 0.5°); the **range** of values used is 10° to 70°; a good choice is to use **evenly spaced** angles.
core.p: AQA expects you to name variables precisely. The **independent variable** is the one you deliberately change, the **dependent variable** is the one you measure as a result, and **control variables** are everything else you keep the same so that it is a fair test. A common mark scheme phrase is 'the only thing that changes is the angle of incidence', and every change that is not controlled makes the results less valid.

bullets: Use a **narrower slit** or a **laser pointer** (with care) to get a thinner ray, so the centre of the beam is easier to mark.
Mark the crosses **as far apart as possible**; a longer line through two widely spaced points gives a more accurate direction than a short line.
Use a **sharp pencil** (thin line) and a **ruler** to draw lines exactly through the crosses.
Read the protractor at **eye level** to avoid parallax error; make sure the **centre mark** of the protractor is exactly at the point of incidence/entry.
**Repeat each measurement** at least 2 or 3 times and calculate a **mean**; this reduces the effect of random errors and helps to spot anomalies.
Use a **darkened room** so the ray is easier to see against the paper.
Use a **protractor with finer divisions** (0.5°) or a **digital angle measurer** to improve resolution.
**Systematic error** example: the protractor zero is not aligned with the normal, or the block moved when you lifted the ray box; this affects all readings in the same way.
**Random error** example: slight variations in marking the crosses; this changes readings unpredictably and can be reduced by repeating.
core.p: Questions on this practical often ask you to suggest **how to improve accuracy**. The main sources of error are the **thickness of the ray**, the **reading of the protractor**, and the **marking of the crosses**. Reducing each of these gives better quality data. Remember: **accuracy** means close to the true value; **precision** means the results are close to each other (repeatable); **resolution** is the smallest division of the measuring instrument.

bullets: **Hazard: ray box lamp gets hot** → can cause **burns** → let it cool before touching, do not touch the lamp housing, and place it away from the edge of the bench.

**Hazard: bright light** (especially if a laser is used) → can **damage eyes** → never look directly into the beam; use a low-power ray box; if a laser is used it must be low power and not pointed at anyone's eyes.
**Hazard: glass block can break and cause cuts** → handle by the edges, place it on the bench away from the edge, and clear any broken glass with a brush and pan (not with fingers).
**Hazard: trailing electrical leads** → can cause trips → keep leads tidy and away from walkways.
**Hazard: working in a dim room** → trip hazard or knocking equipment → keep gangways clear and make sure the room has enough light to move safely.
Use a **low-voltage supply (12 V)** and do not let water touch the mains equipment if using a water block.
Always tell the teacher about **any breakage immediately**.
When writing a risk assessment, give **one hazard, one harm and one precaution**; for example 'the lamp gets hot, so let it cool before moving it to avoid burns'.
core.h: Safety, risk assessment and control measures
core.p: A **risk assessment** names a **hazard**, the **harm** it could cause and a **control measure** to reduce the risk. For this practical the risks are fairly low, but you should still know the specific ones the mark scheme looks for. Never say just 'be careful': you must say exactly what you will do to reduce the risk.

bullets: Table headings: **angle of incidence, i (°)** and **angle of reflection, r (°)** with units in the heading, not in each cell.
Axes: **i on the x-axis, r on the y-axis**; label both with the quantity and unit; use equal scales for both axes for a reflection graph so that the gradient of 1 gives a 45° line.
Draw a **line of best fit**: a straight line through the origin for reflection; a **smooth curve** for r against i in refraction.
Calculate the **gradient** by choosing two points far apart on the line and finding the change in y divided by the change in x: gradient = Δr ÷ Δi.
**Conclusion for reflection:** 'The angle of reflection is equal to the angle of incidence' (for a smooth surface).
**Conclusion for refraction:** 'when light enters glass from air the angle of refraction is smaller than the angle of incidence; as i increases r increases but not in direct proportion'.
**Anomalous results:** point(s) that do not fit the pattern; check for errors, repeat if possible, and exclude if justified.
A **valid conclusion** only refers to the conditions tested: for example, 'for a glass block and a ray of white light between 10° and 70°'.
core.h: Recording data, plotting graphs and drawing conclusions
core.p: A good results table has **headings with units**, the independent variable in the **first column**, and the dependent variable(s) in the next column(s), with repeated readings and a mean if appropriate. For a graph, the **independent variable goes on the x-axis** and the **dependent variable on the y-axis**, with a sensible scale that uses more than half of the grid, plotted points marked with a cross or small circle, and a **line of best fit** (a straight line or smooth curve, not joining the dots). The conclusion must be supported by the data and must state the **pattern** and the **relationship**.

bullets: **Specular reflection:** from a smooth surface, parallel rays reflect as parallel rays in one direction (clear image).
**Diffuse reflection:** from a rough surface, normals point in many directions, so reflected rays scatter (no clear image).
**Matt black** surfaces are good absorbers and poor reflectors; **shiny surfaces** are good reflectors.
For refraction of different substances, compare the same i with different blocks: the **material that slows light more** gives a **smaller r** (the ray bends more towards the normal).
**Glass** bends light more than **water**, so for the same i, r in glass is smaller than r in water.
Light of different **colours** (wavelengths) is refracted by slightly different amounts, with **violet bending most** and **red least** (the basis of dispersion).
If a block is a different **thickness**, the amount of sideways shift of the emergent ray changes but the angles stay the same.
Use the **same angle of incidence** for each material when comparing so the test is fair.
core.h: Comparing different surfaces and different substances
core.p: The specification says 'different types of surface' and 'different substances', so you may be asked to compare materials. The key ideas are that **smooth surfaces give specular reflection**, **rough surfaces give diffuse reflection**, and that **different transparent materials slow light by different amounts**, so they refract it by different amounts. For colour, the surface **absorbs** some wavelengths and **reflects** others, so a red surface reflects mainly red light and absorbs most other colours.

bullets: The practical links to **wave properties** (speed, wavelength, frequency), the **law of reflection**, and **refraction as a change of speed**.
It connects to **lenses** (refraction at curved surfaces), **optical fibres** (total internal reflection, beyond GCSE for AQA), **prisms** and **dispersion**.
Mark schemes want you to say that the angles are measured **from the normal** and that the line of the ray is found by **joining two crosses** with a ruler.

For 'explain the shape of the graph' answers, refer to **proportionality**: reflection gives a straight line through the origin (r = i); refraction gives a curve (r is not directly proportional to i).
Be careful to distinguish **'light speeds up/slows down'** from **'light bends'**: the change in speed is the cause and the bending is the effect.
In 6-mark questions give a **logical sequence**: set-up, measurement, repeat, record, process and conclude.
When asked how to make results more **reliable**, suggest repeating and calculating a mean; for **valid**, suggest controlling variables; for **accurate**, suggest better equipment or technique.
core.h: Exam technique and links to other topics
core.p: Practical questions are worth marks for method detail, variables, safety, accuracy and conclusions. They often use phrases such as 'describe how you would...' or 'a student investigated...'. Always answer with specific steps and numbers (for example 'measure from the normal using a protractor'), and use terms like **independent variable**, **control variable**, **reproducible** and **valid**. Link the results back to the physics (speed changes, bending towards or away from the normal).

exam: **Describe (4 to 6 marks):** give a numbered sequence: draw round block, draw normal, ray at known angle, mark ray with crosses, remove block, join crosses with ruler, measure angles from the normal with a protractor, repeat at different angles.
**Identify variables (1 mark each):** independent = angle of incidence; dependent = angle of refraction; control = same block, same ray box/slit, same colour of light.
**Safety (2 marks):** hazard + precaution, e.g. 'the lamp gets hot, so allow it to cool before moving it'.
**Accuracy (2 marks):** use a narrower slit/thin ray, mark crosses far apart, use a sharp pencil, read the protractor at eye level.
**Reliability (1 to 2 marks):** repeat the readings and calculate a mean; spot and ignore anomalous results.

**Graph questions:** put the independent variable on the x-axis, label axes with units, plot accurately, draw a line of best fit; for reflection state 'straight line through the origin, gradient 1, so r = i'.
**Explain refraction (2 to 3 marks):** 'the wave changes speed', 'so the wavefront changes direction', 'bends towards the normal as it slows down in the glass'.
**Conclusion:** describe the pattern with data, e.g. 'as i increases, r increases but r is always smaller than i for air into glass'.
**Calculation of angles:** if the angle between ray and surface is given, subtract from 90° to get the angle to the normal.
**Ray diagrams:** use a ruler, add arrows to show direction, draw the normal as a dashed line and label i and r.

mistakes.r: The angle of incidence is measured between the incident ray and the normal.
mistakes.w: Measuring the angle of incidence from the surface of the mirror.

mistakes.r: Light refracts because its speed changes when it enters a different medium.
mistakes.w: Light bends because it 'gets pulled' by the glass.

mistakes.r: Entering a denser material (air to glass) the ray bends towards the normal.
mistakes.w: The ray bends away from the normal when entering glass.

mistakes.r: The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways.
mistakes.w: The emergent ray is the same as the incident ray.

mistakes.r: A narrow beam is needed so the path of the ray can be marked accurately.
mistakes.w: A wider beam gives better results.

mistakes.r: The frequency stays the same; the speed and wavelength change.
mistakes.w: The frequency of light changes in glass.

mistakes.r: Name the hazard and the specific precaution, e.g. let the lamp cool to avoid burns.
mistakes.w: Say 'be careful' as a safety precaution.

mistakes.r: Draw a line of best fit (straight line or smooth curve) through the points.
mistakes.w: Join the dots on the graph.

mistakes.r: r is not directly proportional to i, so the graph is a curve.
mistakes.w: The graph for refraction is a straight line through the origin.

summary: AQA 8463 required practical 8: investigate the reflection of light by different types of surface and the refraction of light by different substances, using a ray box, mirrors and transparent blocks. You must carry out the method, measure angles from the normal, record and plot results, name variables and risks, and evaluate the accuracy. It tests both the wave theory (law of reflection, refraction as a change of speed) and working scientifically skills.

terms.d: An imaginary line drawn at 90° to the boundary or surface at the point where a ray strikes it; all angles are measured from it.
The angle between the incident ray and the normal.
The angle between the reflected ray and the normal.
The angle between the refracted ray and the normal.
The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection.
The change in direction of a wave as it passes from one medium to another, caused by a change in the speed of the wave.
Reflection from a smooth surface in which parallel rays are reflected as parallel rays in one direction.
Reflection from a rough surface in which the reflected rays are scattered in many directions.
A light source with a slit that produces a narrow beam of light, used to show the path of a ray.
The point on the surface where the incident ray strikes it.
The ray that leaves the second surface of a transparent block.
The variable that is deliberately changed in an investigation.
The variable that is measured in an investigation.
A variable that is kept the same in an investigation to make it a fair test.
A result that does not fit the pattern of the other results and is likely to be due to error.
The smallest change in the quantity being measured that gives a visible change on the reading of the instrument.
How close a measurement is to the true value.
How close repeated measurements are to each other.
The sideways shift of the emergent ray compared to the line of the incident ray after passing through a parallel-sided block.

worked.q: A student shines a ray of light at a plane mirror so that it makes an angle of 25° with the surface of the mirror. (a) Calculate the angle of incidence. (b) State the angle of reflection. (c) Calculate the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray. (3 marks)
steps: The normal is at 90° to the mirror, so i = 90° − 25° = 65°.
By the law of reflection, r = i = 65°.
The angle between the incident and reflected rays = i + r = 65° + 65° = 130°.

worked.ans: As the angle of incidence increases the angle of refraction increases but is always smaller than i, because the light slows down when it enters the glass and bends towards the normal; r is not directly proportional to i.
worked.q: A student measured the angle of refraction r for different angles of incidence i as a light ray passed from air into a glass block: i = 20°, 30°, 40°, 50°, 60° and r = 13°, 19°, 25°, 31°, 35°. Describe the pattern in the results and explain it. (4 marks)
steps: Pattern: as i increases r increases.
r is always smaller than i, so the ray bends towards the normal.
The relationship is not directly proportional: r ÷ i falls from 0.65 (13/20) to 0.58 (35/60), so the graph is a curve.
Explanation: the light slows down in glass (denser medium), so the wavefront changes direction at the boundary.

worked.ans: Model answer: draw round the block, draw a normal, send a thin ray along a line at known i, mark the emergent ray with crosses, remove block, join entry and exit points to find the refracted ray, measure r from the normal with a protractor, repeat for a range of angles of i (e.g. 20° to 70°), and record i and r in a table. Control the same block, ray box and light colour and take care with the hot lamp.
worked.q: Describe a method to investigate how the angle of refraction depends on the angle of incidence for a rectangular glass block. (6 marks)
steps: Place the block on paper and draw round it; remove it and draw a normal at the point of entry.
Draw an incident ray at 20° to the normal and replace the block.
Shine a thin ray from the ray box along the incident line.
Mark the emergent ray with two crosses; remove the block and join the crosses.
Join the entry point to the exit point to draw the ray inside the block.
Measure i and r from the normal using a protractor; repeat for angles up to 70° and record in a table.
